items.title: SCOTUS lets Big Bend border build proceed — 'build first, litigate later' as a sunk-cost strategy
items.idea: The Court allowed ~500 miles of border work (roads, barriers, cameras, sensors) near Big Bend to proceed during litigation. Fulcrum's point: a court can enjoin a decision in one order, but undoing graded roads and installed sensors needs a plan, appropriations and new contracts. Texas flipped Democratic (Hinojosa) on Nov 3 but can't stop federal work.
items.angle: Execution speed beats legal outcome. Same logic applies to data centers: build before the rules arrive.
items.tweetA: Supreme Court lets construction proceed while the case is pending. Every road graded is a remedy that gets more expensive. Policy by facts on the ground. Watch the same playbook on data centers before the new Congress sits.
items.tweetB: Hinojosa wins Texas, the feds pour concrete anyway. Reversal costs real money; stopping costs nothing. Which side of that asymmetry is your portfolio on? $ACA

items.title: France accuses Iran's IRGC of cyberattacks on supermarket refrigerators; pushes EU sanctions
items.idea: In 'Things happen': France accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of hitting supermarket refrigeration systems and pledged to pursue European sanctions. Separately Trump downplayed renewed strikes on Iran after meeting Qatar's PM.
items.angle: Cold-chain as target: cyber warfare hitting food spoilage is a new inflation transmission channel. Cheap to do, expensive to ignore.
items.tweetA: Iran allegedly going after supermarket refrigerators in France. Not banks, not grid. Food spoilage. If cold chain is a target, it's an inflation shock you can't hedge with oil.
items.tweetB: Oil down on the 'peace trade' while France is accusing the IRGC of cyberattacks on its food supply. Markets are pricing diplomacy; the other side is still running ops.

items.title: 'Agentic CPU' scorecard: Vera leads EPYC by ~20% at peak, only 17% when packed — and Nvidia's 2.2x claim is against Sapphire Rapids
items.idea: Daytona: Vera peaked at 13.3 jobs/sec vs 11.1 for EPYC 9755 (about +20%), 12.7 vs 10.9 fully loaded (+17%). DeepInfra: Vera 1.76x Granite Rapids on a single step, but only 1.33x under load. Nvidia's blog '2.2x vs best x86' is, in DeepInfra's data, against older Sapphire Rapids; vs current EPYC it is 1.2x. No chip passes all five tests.
items.angle: Vendor multiples shrink when benchmarks are independent. Matters for the CPU-for-agents capex narrative — head-node is small share of rack cost.
items.tweetA: Nvidia says Vera is 2.2x the best x86. In the independent data, that 2.2x is against Sapphire Rapids. Against the current EPYC it's 1.2x. Every vendor benchmark has an asterisk; read the baseline.
items.tweetB: Jassy: RL and agent tool use run mostly on CPUs. If that's right the next AI hardware fight isn't GPUs, it's the host chip that keeps them from idling. And the independent numbers say nobody has won it yet. $NVDA $AMD $INTC $ARM

items.title: Arm's '2x per rack' = ~1.2x per chip; AMD Venice (256 cores) and 74,000-thread Helion rack haven't been benchmarked
items.idea: Arm/Signal65: ~2x work per rack vs EPYC 9755; per chip Futurum's read is ~1.2x, with AMD winning 2 of 7 workloads. The rest comes from fitting more servers in a 24kW rack using Arm's own power ratings. AMD claims Venice beats every server CPU per core, per watt and per dollar (no methodology); Helion holds up to 144 Venice, ~74,000 threads, first systems this quarter.
items.angle: The agentic CPU race is a spec-sheet war with no independent data yet. Unproven claims are priced as facts.
items.tweetA: Arm says 2x. Per chip it's 1.2x. The other 0.8x is rack math using Arm's own power numbers. When the benchmark author picks the denominator, the result is a marketing number.
items.tweetB: 74,000 threads in one AMD rack, shipping this quarter, benchmarked by nobody. I'll believe the agent-CPU TAM when someone runs a real workload on it. $AMD $ARM

items.title: WSJ: AI could beat quantum computers to breaking encryption
items.idea: Per WSJ via Parekh: recent AI math breakthroughs on decades-old problems raise the chance AI finds shortcuts in cryptography before quantum does. Skeptics: nobody has shown current encryption is broken; worst case is longer keys. Parekh thinks commercial quantum is a decade-plus away.

items.tweetB: Bitcoin's quantum FUD assumes a hardware breakthrough. What if the attack is a model that finds a shortcut? Different timeline, different mitigation. $BTC

items.title: Binance's $6.3B hack: five-month social-engineering kill chain via an AI coding tool, drained in ~20 minutes, attributed to North Korea
items.idea: Binance report: June, a wallet engineer downloaded a tampered package while installing an AI coding tool. September, a second engineer got a fake recruiter's malware-laden assignment. Oct 20, attackers used that machine plus a Binance internal AI tool to take over two more and found a deploy credential. Nine days later a script reached the wallet-signing system; funds left in ~20 minutes. FBI: North Korea. Attackers controlled signing, not stolen keys. Binance covered 98% of losses; CFO stepped down (says planned).
items.angle: AI dev tooling is now an attack surface. Signing infrastructure, not keys, is the vulnerability for every custodian.
items.tweetA: Five months of patience, 20 minutes of execution. The entry point wasn't a smart contract, it was an AI coding tool installed by an engineer. Your security perimeter now includes whatever your developers let an agent install.
items.tweetB: Binance covered 98% of a $6.3B loss out of pocket. How many exchanges could do that? That's custody concentration risk: only a handful of venues are too big to fail and too big to audit. $BNB $BTC
